name: AI Certifications
blurb: Vendor and vendor-neutral certifications, cost, renewal, and employer recognition.

items.name: AWS Certified AI Practitioner
items.audience: Anyone demonstrating AI literacy on AWS

items.name: AWS Certified Machine Learning - Specialty
items.note: The deep AWS ML credential: data engineering through deployment

items.name: Microsoft Azure AI Engineer Associate (AI-102)
items.audience: Engineers building on Azure AI services

items.name: Databricks Machine Learning certifications
items.note: Associate and Professional ML credentials tied to MLflow-era practice
items.audience: ML engineers on the lakehouse stack

items.name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer
items.note: Google Cloud's ML credential; widely recognized for MLOps depth

items.name: AI Governance Professional (AIGP)
items.note: The vendor-neutral AI governance credential; the governance counterpart to CIPP

items.name: ISO/IEC 42001 Lead Implementer / Lead Auditor
items.note: Credentials against the AI management system standard the compliance section tracks
items.audience: AI management system implementers and auditors

items.name: NVIDIA Certification Program
items.note: Generative AI LLM and infrastructure tracks from the hardware vendor itself

reading.body:
Six of the nine certifications tracked here are issued by cloud infrastructure vendors, AWS, Microsoft, Google, and Databricks, which means most credentialing in this field is tied to a specific vendor's platform rather than to the field as a whole.

Two credentials break that pattern. The IAPP's AI Governance Professional and the ISO/IEC 42001 Lead Implementer and Lead Auditor credentials are vendor-neutral, aimed at governance, compliance, and audit roles rather than at engineers building on a specific cloud. Their existence alongside seven vendor-specific technical credentials shows the field now has two separate credentialing tracks, one for building AI systems and one for governing them, rather than a single certification path.

NVIDIA's certification program is the odd one out, issued by a hardware vendor rather than a cloud platform, which ties directly back to the compute layer underneath every other credential here. The data does not say which of these nine is most commonly held or most valued by employers, only what each covers and who issues it.
